title: Active Directory Basics: the kingdom you'll conquer
description: What a domain is, the Domain Controller, users/groups and how Kerberos authenticates: the corporate forest map.

1.title: Domains and the Domain Controller
1.body:
## From chaos to a domain

Without AD: every machine has its own local users (workgroup) — unmanageable at scale.
With AD: a **domain** (e.g. `corp.local`) centralizes identities. A domain
user signs in on ANY authorized machine: one identity, many machines.

## The DC: the crown jewel

The **Domain Controller (DC)** stores the NTDS.dit database (every
user and every hash) and answers authentication requests. Compromising the DC = compromising the whole
domain. That's why in AD labs your end goal is always to reach the DC.

## The hierarchy

```text
Forest                  ← security boundary
└── Domain corp.local
    ├── OU=Madrid
    │   ├── users, computers, groups
    │   └── applied GPOs
    └── OU=Barcelona
```

**OUs** group objects so you can delegate and apply **GPOs** (Group Policy Objects:
policies the DC pushes to the machines — settings, restrictions, startup
scripts… and sometimes cleartext passwords an attacker will happily read).

## Minimum vocabulary

- **Object**: user, computer, group, printer… anything that lives in AD.
- **Security group**: a collection of users with permissions (Domain Admins is THE
  group you'll want).
- **Trust**: a relationship between domains/forests that allows cross access — in
  Red Teaming, the route to the "parent domain".

2.title: Groups that matter (and why you'll want them)
2.body:
## The groups of the realm

| Group | Power |
|---|---|
| **Domain Admins** | administrators of the whole domain (DC included) |
| **Enterprise Admins** | the whole FOREST (the top level) |
| **Administrators** | local admins on each machine |
| **Domain Users** | any domain user |

In an engagement, your dream escalation is usually: regular user → Domain Admins. And your
nightmare as a defender: someone being in there without you knowing it.

## Kerberos: the guardian with tickets

AD has authenticated with **Kerberos** (port 88) since Windows 2000:

1. **AS-REQ**: you send your username to the **KDC** (a service on the DC).
2. **AS-REP**: you receive a **TGT** (Ticket Granting Ticket) encrypted with your key.
3. **TGS-REQ**: you present the TGT to request access to a service (e.g. a file server).
4. **TGS-REP**: you receive the **service ticket**, which you present to the server.

No password is ever sent over the network — only cryptographic tickets. The attacks
you'll study later (Kerberoasting, Pass-the-Ticket, AS-REP Roasting) abuse
exactly these tickets. For now, remember: **TGT = temporary master key;
service ticket = the key to one specific door**.

> NTLM (the older protocol) is still active in many networks and brings its own abuses
> (NTLM relay). We go deeper, with labs, in the Jr Pentester path.

active-directory-basico-t02-q01.prompt: Which group has full control over ALL domain controllers?

active-directory-basico-t02-q02.prompt: What is the built-in local administrator account on EVERY Windows machine called?
active-directory-basico-t02-q02.hint: The usual one, the one Windows created at install time.

active-directory-basico-t02-q03.prompt: What does a 'ticket' represent in Kerberos authentication?
active-directory-basico-t02-q03.hint: A pass that proves who you are without resending your password.

options.b: A cryptographic proof of identity that you present to services

3.title: Your first look inside AD
3.body:
## LDAP: the language of AD

Active Directory speaks **LDAP** (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol, port 389/636).
Enumerating AD = asking the DC LDAP questions: "give me every user", "who are the
Domain Admins?", "which computers are there?".

```powershell
# From a domain-joined Windows machine, no extra tools:
net user /domain              # domain users
net group "Domain Admins" /domain
```

The historic binary: **net** (yes, net!). For more power you'll use PowerShell
(`Get-ADUser -Filter *`) or offensive tools (enum4linux, BloodHound — the latter
maps complete attack paths and you'll see it in Jr Pentester).

## DNS: the domain's phone book

AD is married to its internal DNS: the `corp.local` domain lives there. The
**SRV** records (`_ldap._tcp.corp.local`) announce which machines are DCs and which services
they offer (Kerberos, LDAP…). That's why "DNS is broken" on a corporate network usually
means "AD is broken".

With this you wrap up the Windows/AD module: editions and the Registry, UAC and the domain
model. Next stop: networking — how your packets really travel.

active-directory-basico-t03-q01.prompt: Which directory protocol does Active Directory use?
active-directory-basico-t03-q01.hint: Successor of X.500; its port is 389.

active-directory-basico-t03-q02.prompt: Which Windows command-line tool queries AD (e.g. to list domain users)?
active-directory-basico-t03-q02.hint: Three letters; you use it with 'user /domain' and 'group /domain'.

active-directory-basico-t03-q03.prompt: What does DNS in an AD domain record besides names (key for finding controllers)?
active-directory-basico-t03-q03.hint: SRV records point to the DCs.

options.a: Nothing: DNS is independent of AD
options.b: SRV records announcing where the DCs and their services are
